1.1: 1.1 Argument. The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians, and they themselves had been forestalled by false apostles, and the Apostle himself did not come to them, but corrects them by letter. For they had heard the word from Archippus, who also received the ministry among them. Therefore the Apostle, already bound, writes to them from Ephesus by Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte. Paul. In his usual manner he sets the greeting first. This premised, he gives thanks for their good, and commending faith and love prays that they may be perfected in Christ, whose benefits and primacy according to both natures he commends; then recalling the dignity of his own ministry he warns them not to be seduced by prophecy or the ceremonies of the law and fall away from Christ; finally he instructs all together morally according to sexes and ages and conditions, and at the end admonishes Archippus to be careful of the ministry he has undertaken. Apostle, etc. Note that rightly here he names himself apostle, because he was apostle also to those to whom he had preached through his disciples.
1.3: 1.3 We give thanks. He shows the goods they received, while he gives thanks for them.
1.6: 1.6 As, etc. That is, as purely and truly as it came through me and others into the whole world, and still abides in it, as if he said: No less was done for you than in the other churches. Since the Gospel is in the world, it bears fruit there by good works, and grows by increase of knowledge and number of the faithful. Not that these have more than you, but God does it so, as it is in you, and therefore you ought to add nothing.
1.7: 1.7 For you, etc. Desiring their salvation, he began to help Archippus.
1.8: 1.8 In the Spirit. Because you love for spiritual things, not for carnal.
1.9: 1.9 That you may be filled in all. It is great to know fully what God wills, in all things of the active life and the contemplative.
1.10: 1.10 In knowledge. That they may not be ignorant of the form of their faith, that is the thing hoped for, whence they will be firm.
1.11: 1.11 In all power. You, I say, strengthened by God in all power, in chastity namely and the rest. Which he can well do who is the brightness of the Father, that is the Son. Or according as he has given you clear knowledge.
1.12: 1.12 Giving thanks. Now he begins to say that the law does not profit, but harms, and Christ suffices for all good: which can be known from this, that he himself and the other apostles (who had been in legal things), leaving them, fled to Christ: as if he said: For you we pray, giving thanks to God, because he makes us worthy, which the law could never do. He has made us worthy. Not in the law, but in light, that is through God who is light from light, by whose grace we are enlightened. Or in light, that is in clear knowledge, from which swerving one falls into darkness. Of the lot. The will of God, in the human race, is the lot with him in whom is no iniquity, but he does all things through justice, even if hidden.
1.13: 1.13 Who has delivered us from the power. That is from hell, in which we were held by the devil: as well from our own as from the fault of Adam. And has translated us, etc. When, lifting us from the depth of Tartarus, he led us into heaven with his only Son. For already believers, who are devout with fixed mind, going out of the world, are led into heaven with the angel of the right hand of the Father as guide. The kingdom of the Son. Of which he himself says: My kingdom is not of this world; he does not say: It is not here, but, it is not from here, because he sojourns indeed in the world, but is not of the world. For to his kingdom he says, You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world. They were of the world when they belonged to the prince of the world.
1.14: 1.14 Redemption. The power of the devil destroyed, the means of liberty was given us by the shedding of the blood of him who had no sin. That, because the devil rightly held those whom he had bound as guilty of sin by the condition of death, he should rightly release them through him whom he undeservedly afflicted with the penalty of death, guilty of no sin.
1.15: 1.15 Who is the image. Otherwise the image of a king is in a coin, otherwise in a son. We are the coin, in whom the image of God is Christ the Son. No image of God ought to be worshiped, except that which is what he himself is, nor that in his place, but with him.
1.18: 1.18 The head of the body, the Church. Because he stands to the Church as the head to the body. And since the Church began from Abel, how is he their head? Well, because he is the beginning of the Church, that is, the founder. Who is the beginning. Of the Church according to the divinity, that is founder of the Church, because he enlightened by the power of his divinity and by the gift of his mercy all the just who are begotten from Abel to the last just one. According to the humanity he can also be called the beginning of the Church, because it is founded on the faith of his humanity. And well is he head and beginning, and ruler, and founder, because he is the firstborn, etc. Firstborn, etc. As he was born before all things of God, that he might create all things, so as man he rises first, that he may restore, that he may always be first and prince.
1.19: 1.19 Fullness. Because he can do all things from himself; whence: As the Father has life in himself, so the Son also, who raises and gives life to whom he will, so he is shown to be perfect God.
1.20: 1.20 To reconcile through him. It pleased God to reconcile through him, and he made peace not freely, but through blood, things heavenly and earthly, whence the entrance into heaven is open to man. All things were made through him, and in him as author they live.
1.21: 1.21 Alienated and enemies in mind, which comes to the same, because they did not receive what God commanded through Moses, as being devoted to their idols.
1.22: 1.22 He has reconciled in the body. If mortal and dead he could reconcile, now immortal he can do all things.
1.23: 1.23 If you continue. Therefore he had said so many and so great things of Christ, that they may place hope in him alone, in whom are all things; let them not think that they must subject themselves to any of the elements or angels: this one alone is to be worshiped, and to him no one is to be compared. In all. The new creature which is now under heaven is still a pilgrim, yet will come to glory.
1.24: 1.24 I fill up. Those of the sufferings which Christ endured, or which he now commanded to endure, which are still lacking, I fill up, that is I am ready to suffer.
1.25: 1.25 Whereof I am made. He says he was made minister of the Gospel by God through Christ, that the ministry begun by God may be fulfilled through a fit servant, which was unknown from ages. Which is given to me. That I may fulfill what God foreordained about you, namely that you be saved through the incarnation. He says this lest it seem that salvation was not promised to the Gentiles. Or, given to me in you, for so much is sought of mine as if from myself.
1.28: 1.28 Admonishing. Those who contradict we rebuke and overcome, and the obedient we teach. In all wisdom. True wisdom is when Christ is acknowledged. That we may present, etc. In whom. As if he said: To my labor God adds miracles for confirmation.
2.1: 2.1 For I would, etc. It follows: For you. For the Apostle was no less solicitous for those he had not seen than for those he had seen.
2.2: 2.2 Instructed in charity. Which God had toward us, who delivered his Son for us. Unto all riches. That is the abundance of full understanding, where they may have perfectly understanding of human and divine things, as of the soul and of the higher spirits. For otherwise no one ascends to the knowledge of God. Of God the Father, etc. That you may know that the Father is another person from the Son, though the same in substance with him. If you aim at knowledge, run back to Christ alone, because in him are all the riches, but hidden, and therefore do not wonder if you are in Christ and have not yet found them, because they are not open to all, but to those who ask and knock.
2.4: 2.4 And this. I do not say only that you should reach after what you do not yet have, but that no one deceive you and, by reason of worldly things, draw you away from the hope which is in Christ.
2.5: 2.5 For though in spirit. To the saints it is given in spirit to see things far off. Let those take care therefore whose acts are not hidden from the master. Rejoicing. By this he makes them readier toward the Gospel, because he says he rejoices in the arrangement of their conduct and the steadiness of their faith, that knowing why they please God they may become firmer in him.
2.7: 2.7 Rooted. The lesser in the active life. Built up over others in him. That is you greater who are in contemplation.
2.8: 2.8 Deceit. What the false preachers say about the law. And vain. Because in this falsehood there is no profit, which is wont sometimes to be in falsehoods. According to the elements. He touches those who more prudently explain the idols, saying, Juno is air, Neptune the sea; therefore when he said according to philosophy and vain, he adds, according to the elements of the world: as if admonishing us to beware not only of worshipers of images of any sort, but also of teachers and interpreters of signs.
2.9: 2.9 Bodily. Not that God is corporeal, but he used a figurative word, because in the temple made with hands he dwelt not bodily but in shadow, that is by prefiguring signs. Bodily, because in the body of Christ which he took of the Virgin God dwells as in a temple, but not so in the saints, because that is the head in which all the senses abide; as the touch alone, to whom the spirit is given by measure, of whom it cannot be said: The Word was made flesh, John 1, nor is any of them called only-begotten of God.
2.12: 2.12 Buried with him. That is baptized in the likeness of his burial. Through the faith of the operation. That is by believing the works of God. He explains one of the works of God, which it is especially necessary for those who wish to rise to believe, namely that God raised Christ, and that by Christ's example he will raise them, whence he adds: Who raised him, etc.
2.14: 2.14 Blotting out. Not only to you Gentiles has God given, but to us Jews also he has remitted the transgressions which are from the law. And this, Blotting out. Handwriting. He speaks of the sin of Adam, which he took away and nailed to the cross, but not that alone: because unless he took away this and the others, we should not be freed from death and hell. While the innocent is killed, sin is crucified. Decree, is the sentence adverse among all men, by which it was said: You shall die the death, etc. Nailing it. That it may now cease, when all the sacrifices are fulfilled in the offering of the true Lamb.
2.15: 2.15 Despoiling principalities and powers. By taking away Abraham, Isaac and the other just. He led them away, far from this kingdom to heaven. Confidently. That is with hope of victory. Triumphing, that is overcoming them on the cross, which is not in secret but openly. For if one regards the perfection of the Church, the ancient enemy is plainly seen conquered. Or, he led away principalities and powers, that is he drove them out of the Church. Triumphing over them in himself. By his death. By one truest sacrifice offered for us, whatever of faults there was (by which principalities and powers held us to pay the penalties of life), he extinguished: whence therefore the devil received outwardly power to kill the Lord's flesh, thence the inner power of his which held us was killed.
2.17: 2.17 Which are a shadow, etc. Then there were precepts of this kind, which not to keep was sin, now testimonies and confirmation of the truth. The Scripture which then was exactor of works that signified, is now witness of the things signified: and what was then observed for foretelling, is now recited for confirmation. But the body. That is, the truth of this shadow is Christ's, that is, pertains to Christ. Or all those are the body of Christ, that is signify the body of Christ, either that which he took of the Virgin, or the Church.
2.18: 2.18 Willing. That is loving what he has not seen. Or, willing namely to persuade what he has not seen, namely the ceremonies of the law whose reason he does not know. Puffed up. The puffed-up understands nothing else than sensuality takes in.
2.19: 2.19 Compacted, etc. Into one by joining, because they believe the same, and do the same things. And ministered in subserving. By the bands. That is by charity, without which the members do not cohere, nor serve one another, nor live. Unto the increase of God. God is increased by those returning, as he is diminished by those deserting.
2.20: 2.20 If then you be dead. So far he has warned those standing not to be seduced, now he attacks those who already kept some of the law; as if he said: See that you are not seduced, but tell others why you keep the law? He calls elements the creatures of this world. If, he says, when you received the faith of Christ, you are separated from sin, and from the elements of the world, that is from abstinence, and from all superstition of the creatures of the world. Why still, etc. It can be taken with Christ and as Christ.
2.22: 2.22 Which all by use itself, etc. If anyone uses them in the Jewish rite, so as to abstain from these, use those, believing to be justified thereby, they lead to death. These I say already existing according to the precepts and doctrines of men, etc., not of God: for after the truth came, now God does not command these, but the Pharisees command them by authority, and teach by reasons.
2.23: 2.23 In humility, etc. The humility here understood is not that which is a virtue, but as understood from the Greek, that by which the mind thinks lowly, that is useful and earthly things, that is by dejection of soul, and they are: Not to spare the body. Because in those observances there is much labor, which is vain, and they are not: In honor of God, whose counsel is called void, nor of the saints, whose faith is destroyed, and they are not: To the satisfying of the flesh, because they withdraw many things. In superstition, etc. Religion is feigned that false things may seem true, which humbles minds on earth lest they be raised to the heights; and it harms the body, whose head is Christ: not in honor because, having Christ the head cut off, they fulfill the sense of the flesh. For fattening is carnal sense human tradition, because it says that suffices which the prudence of the flesh hands down.
3.1: 3.1 Seek the things that are above. Not by place, but by merit of excellence.
3.2: 3.2 Mind the things that are above. Spiritual, which were signified through carnal observances, these are, eternal glory and what leads to it.
3.3: 3.3 Your life is hid. That is, your time has not yet come, because summer has not yet come, that is the coming of Christ, where fruitful trees will be discerned from barren; but the time of those who love earthly things is always ready. When Christ shall appear, this is our time.
3.5: 3.5 Mortify, etc. After the reasons concerning the fullness of Christ, a general exhortation to all about morals is added, lest they return to the former custom. Your members. That is the parts of the old man, or the concupiscences of the members. Fornication, etc. He describes the offenses which he calls members, that after receiving the reason of truth they may give attention to a good life. It greatly harms to know the reason of the truth, and not to follow it in deeds. For he who knows the will of the Lord and does it not, shall be beaten with many stripes, Luke 12. And covetousness. Under one name he forbids two worst things, idolatry and covetousness, which is not unlike malice, because the root of all evils, and almost fulfilled by one work: because as idolatry strives to take from the one God his glory, that he alone may not have the name of deity, so the covetous man stretches himself against God's things, that he alone may usurp what God made for all: each is hostile to God, because they deny God what is his.
3.7: 3.7 In which you also walked. This delays me that they may rejoice to have escaped it and for the rest take care.
3.8: 3.8 But now. Above he forbade graver things, now lesser, lest these be thought not dangerous. There are those who have not the habit of drunkenness, who sometimes get drunk: as there are also those who have not the habit of lying, and yet sometimes lie, so too with others. He forbids therefore sometimes to lie, and especially to lie constantly.
3.10: 3.10 Who is renewed. The renewal of the mind is said according to God, as is read in the epistle to the Ephesians, or according to the image of God, as is read here. But therefore according to God, lest it be thought to be made according to another creature.
3.14: 3.14 Charity. For it is the more eminent way which surpasses knowledge and all precepts. This is the seamless garment of the Lord woven from above. Seamless, lest it ever be unstitched, which comes to one, because charity gathers all into one.
3.15: 3.15 Peace. This is necessary for the unity of the body, which it made. The peace of God. That can be called peace which has not charity; but charity always has peace with it.
3.16: 3.16 Teaching and admonishing. He says this, that there may be teaching for those who do not know, and admonition for those who know.
3.17: 3.17 All whatsoever. Because he commanded above that God be praised in the heart, now he exhorts that the name of God be praised and exalted in words and in deeds: that so our words and works be free from reproach, that the Lord may be magnified, by whose teaching the disciples are blameless. All. Not only what you do in word or work, but all, even thoughts, and whatever else there is. Or whatever you do, do all, that is perfect, ascribing it to God, and this is, doing in the name. Giving thanks. Then we truly give thanks to God through Christ, if we keep the measure of his precepts.
3.21: 3.21 Fathers. He commands fathers to be moderate with their sons, lest, constrained by them, they offend against them, and offend God. For anger is an inconsiderate thing, so that sometimes he who is angry does not spare even himself.
3.23: 3.23 Whatsoever you do, do it from the heart as to the Lord. God approves that innocence by which a man is innocent not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness: for he who does not sin from fear, though he harm no others, yet harms himself very much. Feigned equity is not equity, but doubled sin. In which is iniquity and pretense.
4.3: 4.3 A door. That is, may he make my mouth open: which was given for this, that the word may come out from it. It is open when it says many and great things.
4.5: 4.5 Redeeming the time. That is preparing in some ways the opportunity of preaching to them.
4.8: 4.8 That he may know the things that concern you and comfort your hearts, etc. He takes more care who sees himself known than he who sees himself unknown.
4.10: 4.10 You have received, which has returned to me, and therefore if he come.
4.16: 4.16 See that in the, etc. From this place we understand that the instructions of the Apostle are general, and that the epistles were written for the progress of all men.
4.18: 4.18 Remember, etc. Before he puts the greeting, he sets first an exhortation saying: Remember, etc.
